prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A new company in Germany is trying to break into the fashion business selling stylish clothes designed and produced by prison inmates. Inmates design and produce the Haeftling range. The company Haeftling, which in English means inmate, has just opened its first store in Berlin. "We want to have basic, durable, timeless, beautiful clothes," said Stephan Bohle, one of the company founders. Many of the clothes, cooking aprons and even stainless steel food trays offered in the Berlin store were either designed or manufactured in jails, but not just German ones. One design shows a female comic figure that was drawn by a man sitting on death row in Texas. Bohle said part of the proceeds from sales go to organizations that support prisoners' rights and better conditions for inmates, like Amnesty International. But in some cases, money goes directly to the inmates that designed certain pieces. "In the case of the female cartoon figure, this man was almost granted a stay from execution because of the design he did for us but in the end unfortunately the appeals court ruled against him," Bohle said . The clothes offered at the Haeftling shop also tell the story of the inmates that designed individual pieces. A small text inside the item lays out the prisoners story, including the name, where he is in jail and how long the term will be. Some of the clothes are manufactured at a corrections facility in Halle, near Leipzig, in Eastern Germany.  Watch the inmates at work » . Prisoners sew cooking aprons in a jail workshop for several hours a day. "It's wonderful, at least it takes your mind off jail for a little while," says Mario Hildebrand, who is serving a 20 month term in Halle. "We can really identify with this label," he said. "We are the prisoners and without us this label would not be possible, so we do take some pride in making these clothes." However, Mario said he would not wear the clothes himself: "Look, I am a prisoner, and I'm really not proud of it. It isn't something I want to be parading around." But others seem to be catching the fever. Bohle said the company wants to start selling in the United States. "We've had people from New York, Chicago and Los Angeles ask about Haeftling," he said in an interview in the flagship store in Berlin. Bohle said he hopes socially responsible clothes will also make for a good business for the company. E-mail to a friend .

“In the case of the female cartoon figure, this man was almost granted a stay of execution because of the design he created for us, but unfortunately, the appeals court ultimately ruled against him,” Bohle said.

The clothing sold at the Haeftling store also tells the stories of the inmates who designed individual pieces. A short text inside each item recounts the prisoner’s story, including the inmate’s name, place of incarceration, and length of sentence.

Some of the clothing is manufactured at a correctional facility in Halle, near Leipzig in eastern Germany. [Watch the inmates at work »]

Prisoners spend several hours a day sewing cooking aprons in a prison workshop.

“It’s wonderful; at least it takes your mind off prison for a little while,” said Mario Hildebrand, who is serving a 20-month sentence in Halle.

“We can really identify with this label,” he said. “We are the prisoners, and without us, this label would not be possible, so we do take some pride in making these clothes.”

However, Mario said he would not wear the clothing himself. “Look, I am a prisoner, and I’m really not proud of it. It isn’t something I want to parade around.”

Others, however, appear to be catching the enthusiasm. Bohle said the company plans to begin selling its products in the United States.

“We’ve had people from New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles ask about Haeftling,” he said in an interview at the company’s flagship store in Berlin.

Bohle said he hopes that socially responsible clothing will also prove to be good business for the company.

A German start-up is entering the fashion industry with a collection of stylish garments created and made by prisoners. The brand is called Haeftling—the German word for “inmate”—and has recently launched its first retail outlet in Berlin.

Company co-founder Stephan Bohle said the goal is to offer clothing that is simple, attractive, long-lasting and unlikely to go out of style. The Berlin shop sells garments, kitchen aprons and even stainless-steel meal trays. Many of these products were designed or produced in correctional facilities, both in Germany and abroad.

One item features a female comic-book character drawn by a man on death row in Texas. According to Bohle, some sales revenue is donated to groups such as Amnesty International that campaign for prisoners’ rights and improved prison conditions. In other instances, the inmates responsible for particular designs receive money directly.

Bohle said the Texas prisoner who created the female cartoon image came close to receiving a stay of execution because of his work for the company. Ultimately, however, the appeals court ruled against him.

Haeftling’s clothing also provides information about the prisoners behind individual products. A short passage printed inside each piece gives the inmate’s name, the prison where he is being held and the length of his sentence.

Some items are produced at a correctional institution in Halle, near Leipzig in eastern Germany. There, prisoners spend several hours each day sewing kitchen aprons in a prison workshop.

Mario Hildebrand, who is serving a 20-month sentence in Halle, said the work is valuable because it allows inmates to stop thinking about prison for a while. He added that the prisoners feel closely connected to Haeftling: the brand could not exist without them, and they take pride in producing its clothes.

Nevertheless, Hildebrand said he would not personally wear the label. He explained that although he is a prisoner, it is not an identity he is proud of or wishes to display publicly.

The brand appears to be attracting interest elsewhere. Bohle said Haeftling hopes to begin selling its products in the United States and has already received inquiries from people in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Speaking at the company’s flagship Berlin store, he said he hopes its socially responsible approach to clothing will also prove commercially successful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news article about Haeftling, a German fashion company that sells clothing designed and manufactured by prison inmates.
counterfactuals.output:
# German Fashion Label Haeftling Turns Prison Workshops Into a Clothing Brand

**BERLIN —** A German fashion company is drawing attention to an unusual production model: clothing designed and manufactured with the help of prison inmates.

Haeftling — a German word meaning “prisoner” or “inmate” — sells casual clothing and other goods produced in correctional facilities. The label, also known as Haeftling Jailwear, began in the early 2000s and has marketed items such as T-shirts, jackets, trousers and accessories with a deliberately austere, prison-inspired aesthetic.

The company works with prison workshops, where inmates sew garments and participate in other stages of production. Supporters of the model say such work can provide structure, practical experience and vocational skills that may help prisoners find employment after their release.

Haeftling also presents its German manufacturing base as an alternative to the fashion industry’s reliance on low-cost overseas production. The brand’s identity emphasizes durable materials, straightforward designs and the story behind the people making the products.

But the business model has also raised questions about prison labor. In Germany, incarcerated workers generally receive compensation well below wages in the regular labor market and are not covered by all of the same employment protections as workers outside prison. Critics argue that private companies can benefit from a workforce with limited bargaining power.

Advocates of prison employment counter that inmates often value the opportunity to work, earn money and build experience. They say the central issue is whether prison labor is voluntary, fairly organized and connected to meaningful training rather than used simply to reduce production costs.

Haeftling’s branding adds another layer to the debate. Its name and prison-themed image make incarceration a central selling point, prompting questions about whether the company challenges stereotypes or commercializes them.

The label nonetheless occupies a distinctive place in Germany’s fashion sector. By bringing prison-made products into the consumer market, Haeftling has made rehabilitation, labor rights and ethical manufacturing part of the conversation surrounding an otherwise ordinary piece of clothing.

counterfactuals.output:
**Haeftling**—usually styled **HÆFTLING**, German for “prisoner”—is a Berlin label launched in the early 2000s that markets durable, minimalist “jailwear” and household goods made through German prison workshops.

- **Prisoners’ role:** Inmates in participating prisons cut, sew, assemble, print, or package products such as shirts, jackets, underwear, bags, and linens. Professional designers and the Berlin business develop and market the collection; the prison workshops manufacture to those specifications.
- **Payment and proceeds:** Prisoners do not receive a share of the retail profit. They are paid the legally prescribed prison wage—only a fraction of ordinary outside wages—with some money available during imprisonment and some potentially reserved for release. Haeftling pays the prisons for production; workshop revenue goes to the relevant prison or state justice administration to cover costs and support prison operations. The private company retains its commercial margin. Claims that all sales proceeds go directly to inmates, charities, or crime victims are therefore misleading.
- **What inmates say:** Accounts are mixed but often pragmatic. Many value the work because it gets them out of their cells, structures the day, provides training, and gives them pride in producing something sold outside. At the same time, inmates and prison-rights advocates criticize the very low pay, lack of normal labor protections and pension contributions, and the fact that the brand can charge normal retail prices while the makers receive prison-level wages.

The brand presents the arrangement as rehabilitation through skilled work; critics see an uneasy combination of useful vocational activity and inexpensive captive labor.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a CNN-style business and human-interest story on a German startup trying to enter the fashion industry with stylish, durable clothes made in prisons.
counterfactuals.output:
# From cellblock to street style: The German startup betting on prison-made fashion

**Berlin, Germany** — Inside a German prison workshop, the soundtrack of daily life is less about clanging cell doors than the steady rhythm of sewing machines.

Here, incarcerated workers cut heavy cotton, reinforce seams and stitch together shirts, jackets and trousers designed to survive years of wear. The clothes are bound not for prison uniforms or government warehouses, but for consumers searching for an alternative to disposable fashion.

A German startup is betting that prison workshops — long associated with basic furniture, license plates and institutional clothing — can produce garments stylish enough to compete on the high street.

Its pitch is straightforward: minimalist designs, durable materials and local manufacturing, combined with work that can teach prisoners practical skills.

But turning that idea into a mainstream fashion label is complicated. The company must overcome the stigma attached to prison-made goods, operate within the restrictions of correctional facilities and answer difficult questions about how incarcerated workers are paid.

## Selling durability, not novelty

The startup’s clothing is deliberately understated. Instead of chasing seasonal trends, it focuses on workwear-inspired pieces, neutral colors and thick fabrics. The goal is to persuade customers to buy fewer items and keep them longer.

That approach puts the business in step with a wider shift in fashion. Consumers concerned about textile waste and overseas supply chains are increasingly looking for products that claim to be local, traceable and built to last.

Prison workshops offer some advantages. Germany already has a network of correctional facilities equipped for manufacturing, and many run vocational programs intended to prepare inmates for life after release.

Yet prisons are not ordinary factories. Security checks can delay deliveries of fabric and equipment. Production schedules can be disrupted by lockdowns, transfers or staffing shortages. Workers may leave a workshop with little notice.

For a young clothing company, those uncertainties can make it difficult to promise the speed and consistency retailers expect.

## Work behind walls

For prisoners, workshop jobs can provide structure in a place where time often feels abstract. Sewing requires concentration and repetition, but also precision. A crooked pocket or weak seam can make an entire garment unsellable.

Supporters of prison industries argue that such work builds habits valued by employers: arriving on time, following production standards, cooperating with colleagues and taking responsibility for a finished product.

The benefits can extend beyond technical training. Producing something that will be worn — and paid for — outside prison can offer a rare connection to everyday society.

The startup hopes that connection will become part of the garment’s appeal. Each item carries a story not only about where it was made, but about the people trying to rebuild their lives while making it.

That story, however, must be handled carefully. Marketing that leans too heavily on prison imagery risks turning incarceration into a novelty — or using prisoners’ circumstances as a branding device.

## The question of pay

The most sensitive issue is compensation.

Prison wages in Germany are generally far below pay for comparable work outside. Incarcerated workers also do not always receive the same pension and social-security protections as employees in the conventional labor market. Rules differ according to the state and the type of facility.

Critics say companies can benefit from a captive, low-cost workforce whose bargaining power is limited. They argue that vocational training cannot justify compensation that would be unacceptable elsewhere.

Advocates counter that prison workshops have additional costs and restrictions, and that shutting them down would remove one of the few opportunities inmates have to earn money, develop skills and spend productive time outside their cells.

For the startup, the debate creates both a moral and a commercial challenge. Customers attracted by ethical production may scrutinize prison labor even more closely than factories abroad. Transparency about wages, working conditions, training and the company’s profit margins is therefore essential.

## A difficult label to wear

Prison-made goods are not new in Germany. Correctional facilities have produced furniture, baked goods, household products and clothing for decades. What is new is the effort to present those products as desirable fashion rather than institutional merchandise.

That means competing on more than a compelling backstory.

The stitching must be clean. Sizing must be consistent. Deliveries must arrive on time. And the clothes must look good enough that customers would buy them even without the prison connection.

The startup’s larger ambition is to change how people think about both clothing and incarceration: a jacket can be more than a seasonal purchase, and a prisoner can be more than the crime that brought them behind bars.

Whether that message can support a profitable fashion business remains uncertain. The industry is crowded, customer loyalty is elusive and producing within prisons adds layers of bureaucracy that most startups never face.

But in the workshop, the immediate measure of success is simpler. A finished garment is inspected, folded and prepared to leave the prison — carrying with it a small piece of work from a place most consumers will never see.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Haeftling’s first store in Berlin and its plans to expand to the United States. Include quotes from co-founder Stephan Bohle and inmate worker Mario Hildebrand.
counterfactuals.output:
Haeftling—German for “inmate”—opened its first physical store in Berlin after initially building its business online. The label sells prison-inspired clothing and practical goods, including shirts, underwear, bags and shoes, much of it produced by inmates in German correctional facilities. Its stark branding emphasizes where the products come from rather than concealing it.

Co-founder Stephan Bohle said the company aimed to create “an international brand using the credibility and authenticity of prison.” After proving the concept in Germany and attracting interest from foreign customers, Haeftling began seeking business partners in the United States, with plans to establish retail and distribution there. Bohle described America as “the motherland of prisons,” making it a natural—if provocative—market for the label.

For participating prisoners, the work offered both paid employment and a connection with life beyond the institution. Inmate worker Mario Hildebrand said: “I’m proud when I see the products outside and know that I made them.” He added that the work made inmates feel “somehow connected to the outside world.”

Haeftling presented the venture as a commercial fashion business rather than a charity, although it also argued that marketable work experience could help inmates develop skills and self-respect before release. The planned U.S. expansion was intended to turn the Berlin experiment into a broader international brand.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an article examining socially responsible prison-made fashion, focusing on Haeftling’s inmate-designed garments, prisoner stories printed inside the clothes, manufacturing at a Halle correctional facility, and the ethical mission behind the brand.
counterfactuals.output:
# Haeftling: Can Prison-Made Fashion Be Socially Responsible?

Fashion labels usually build identity through celebrity endorsements, seasonal trends, or carefully staged ideas of rebellion. Haeftling takes a more literal approach. Its identity comes from prison: garments are developed with inmates, produced at a correctional facility in Halle, Germany, and printed with stories that bring the experiences of incarcerated people into direct contact with the wearer.

The concept is provocative by design. Even the name—*Häftling*, German for “prisoner” or “inmate”—asks consumers to confront a population that society usually keeps out of sight. Yet Haeftling’s significance depends on more than its prison aesthetic. The brand presents itself as a social project intended to give prisoners meaningful work, creative participation, and a voice beyond the institution.

## Clothing Designed From the Inside

A defining feature of Haeftling is that prisoners are not treated solely as anonymous factory labor. Inmates contribute ideas for garments, graphics, and details, allowing their perspectives to shape the collection.

That participation changes the meaning of the clothes. Workwear references, restrained colors, institutional typography, and functional silhouettes are not simply borrowed as fashion motifs; they emerge from engagement with people who know prison life firsthand. The resulting pieces occupy an uneasy space between streetwear, uniform, and social commentary.

For incarcerated participants, design can also offer something prison routines often restrict: individual expression. A sketch, phrase, or garment concept provides a way to communicate taste and personality in an environment built around standardization. It can also introduce practical experience in product development and manufacturing—skills that may have value after release.

The ethical strength of this model lies in meaningful authorship. If inmate participation is substantive, credited, and fairly recognized, the clothing becomes a form of collaboration rather than a commercial appropriation of prison imagery.

## Stories Hidden Inside the Garments

Haeftling’s most distinctive storytelling device is found inside the clothes. Prisoner accounts are printed on interior surfaces, labels, or linings, placing personal narratives against the wearer’s body.

The placement is important. These stories are not displayed as slogans for passersby. They are encountered privately when a garment is put on, removed, or turned inside out. That intimacy encourages the customer to see the person behind the product—not merely an offender, a case number, or a source of labor.

The accounts can touch on incarceration, regret, family separation, hope, and plans for life after prison. Rather than pretending that prisoners are either monsters or uncomplicated victims, the format allows for more human ambiguity. Responsibility for harm can coexist with the possibility of change.

Printing these narratives inside clothing also reverses fashion’s usual logic. Most brands hide the labor that made their products. Haeftling places the makers’ voices within the product itself. The garment becomes both an object for sale and a portable record of a life that would otherwise remain behind prison walls.

There is nevertheless an ethical obligation in using such stories. Consent must be genuine, privacy protected, and participation free from pressure. Personal testimony should not become another raw material extracted from people with limited power. The difference between amplification and exploitation depends on how stories are selected, edited, credited, and compensated.

## Made at the Halle Correctional Facility

Haeftling garments are associated with production at a correctional facility in Halle. Manufacturing within the prison connects the brand’s public message to actual employment behind bars: inmates take part in making the products rather than serving merely as inspiration for an outside fashion company.

Prison workshops can provide structure, technical training, and a break from the monotony of confinement. Sewing and garment production require precision, patience, quality control, and cooperation. Ideally, these are transferable abilities that can support employment and reintegration after release.

Local prison production may also offer a degree of supply-chain visibility that is uncommon in fashion. Instead of outsourcing to distant factories whose conditions are difficult to verify, the brand can identify where the garments are made and explain who is involved.

But a prison location does not automatically make manufacturing ethical. Incarcerated workers have far less bargaining power than workers outside prison. They may lack ordinary employment protections, freedom to change jobs, or the ability to negotiate wages. Any claim of social responsibility must therefore be measured against concrete questions:

- Is the work voluntary?
- How are inmates paid, and who benefits from the sale price?
- Do participants receive recognized training or qualifications?
- Are health, safety, and working conditions independently monitored?
- Can prisoners decline publicity or storytelling without losing work?
- Does the program provide support that remains useful after release?

Transparency on these issues is essential. “Made in prison” can signal rehabilitation, but it can also conceal cheap and coercive labor. The setting makes scrutiny more—not less—important.

## Fashion as a Bridge to the Outside

Haeftling’s broader mission is to reduce the distance between prisoners and the public. Prisons are designed to separate, and that physical separation often produces moral simplification. People outside may think of inmates only in terms of their convictions; incarcerated people may feel that they have been permanently excluded from ordinary social life.

A garment can function as a modest bridge across that divide. By wearing something designed and made by prisoners, and by reading a story printed inside it, a customer participates in an encounter that would otherwise be unlikely. The product asks whether punishment must also mean invisibility and whether rehabilitation is possible without opportunities to practice responsibility, creativity, and work.

The brand’s mission also challenges the fashion industry’s conventional definition of value. Haeftling does not rely only on fabric, cut, or exclusivity. It attaches value to social context: who designed the garment, who made it, and what kind of future the work is intended to support.

That approach fits within a broader understanding of responsible fashion. Sustainability is not only environmental. It also concerns dignity, labor rights, social inclusion, and the distribution of power along a supply chain.

## The Ethical Tension Is Part of the Product

Haeftling should not be treated as automatically virtuous simply because it involves prisoners. The prison system creates an extreme imbalance of power, and a socially minded brand can still benefit from that imbalance. Nor should consumers assume that buying a shirt constitutes rehabilitation in itself.

The project’s credibility rests on whether incarcerated participants receive meaningful benefits: fair recognition, voluntary involvement, useful skills, appropriate compensation, and control over their personal stories. Clear reporting about these conditions would allow customers to distinguish genuine social enterprise from cause-based marketing.

At its best, Haeftling offers an alternative to both hidden prison labor and superficial “prison chic.” The inmates are visible as designers, makers, and narrators. The Halle workshop becomes not merely a low-cost production site but a potential place of training and creative contribution. The stories inside the garments insist that the people who make them have identities extending beyond their sentences.

Haeftling’s central proposition is that clothing can carry more than a logo. It can carry testimony, responsibility, and the possibility of return. Whether that proposition succeeds depends on rigorous ethical practice—but it offers a compelling model of fashion as a conversation between people inside prison and the society to which most will eventually come back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
